lessons.title: Rework Tools and Equipment
lessons.body:
To fix electronics, you need the right tools. In many African workshops, a basic rework station costs between $50 and $150. Start with a temperature-controlled soldering iron (adjustable 200â450Â°C), a hot air rework station (100â500Â°C), and a desoldering pump (manual or electric). You also need fine tweezers, a flux pen, solder wick (1â2mm), isopropyl alcohol (99%), and a brass sponge for cleaning tips. A magnifying lamp or a smartphone with a macro lens helps for small parts.

For power, ensure your iron matches your local voltage (220â240V in most African countries). Use a surge protector; power fluctuations can damage heating elements. If you often work on through-hole boards, a desoldering gun (like the Hakko FR-301) saves time, but a $5 manual pump works for occasional jobs. For surface-mount (SMD) work, hot air is essential. Practice on scrap boards before touching customer devices.

Keep a multimeter (budget $10â$20) to check continuity and voltages. A cheap USB microscope ($20â$40) lets you inspect solder joints on your phone. Store tips tinned with solder to prevent oxidation. In humid coastal areas, keep silica gel packets in your tool case to avoid rust.

Safety first: work in a ventilated area, wear safety glasses, and never touch the hot air nozzle. Use a fume extractor or a small fan blowing away from you. Solder contains lead in some regions; wash hands after handling. Label your tools and keep them cleanâdirty tips transfer heat poorly and damage pads.

Finally, a good workbench light and an anti-static mat (or a clean cotton cloth) reduce static damage. If you cannot afford a hot air station, a paint stripper heat gun with a nozzle can work for removing large ICs, but control is harder. Start with quality basics and upgrade as you earn.

lessons.title: Desoldering Techniques
lessons.body:
Desoldering is removing solder to free a component or clean a pad. The goal is to heat the joint quickly and remove solder without lifting pads or burning the board. For through-hole parts, use a desoldering pump. Heat the joint with your iron (set to 350Â°C for leaded solder, 380Â°C for lead-free) for 1â2 seconds, then quickly place the pump nozzle over the joint and release. Repeat if needed. Add fresh solder firstâit helps heat transfer.

For surface-mount parts, use hot air. Set the temperature to 300â350Â°C and airflow to low (2â3 on a 1â8 scale). Apply flux to the joint, then move the nozzle in small circles around the component. Once solder melts, lift the part with tweezers. Never force it. For small two-pin parts like resistors, you can use two irons or a specialized tweezers iron.

Solder wick (desoldering braid) is best for cleaning pads. Place the wick over the pad, press with your iron, and the solder will flow into the wick. Add flux to the wick for better results. Use a fresh section of wick each time. For large ground planes, you may need a higher wattage iron (60W+) or preheat the board with a hot air station at 100Â°C.

If a pad is stubborn, add more solder (yes, add) to increase thermal mass, then remove it all at once. In Africa, where humidity can cause oxidation, clean the joint with isopropyl alcohol before desoldering. Avoid overheatingâif the pad turns dark or lifts, stop. Practice on old circuit boards from broken TVs or radios.

After desoldering, clean the area with alcohol and a brush. Inspect for leftover solder balls that can cause shorts. A desoldering pump with a silicone tip (like the Engineer SS-02) is more effective than cheap plastic ones. Always tin your iron tip before and after use.

lessons.title: Component Removal and Replacement
lessons.body:
Removing a component without damaging the board is a skill. For through-hole resistors or capacitors, heat one leg at a time while gently pulling from the other side. Use a small flat screwdriver or tweezers to lift the leg as solder melts. For ICs with many pins, use hot air. Apply flux, heat the whole area evenly, and lift the chip with a vacuum pen or tweezers. Never pry it off.

For SMD two-terminal parts (resistors, capacitors), use two soldering irons or a hot air station. Heat both ends simultaneously and lift with tweezers. For multi-pin ICs (SOIC, QFN), hot air is best. Direct the nozzle around the chip, not on top, to avoid blowing it away. Once solder melts, the chip will floatâlift it straight up. Clean pads with wick and alcohol.

Replacement: First, clean the pads. Apply fresh solder to one pad, then place the new component with tweezers. Solder one pin to hold it, then solder the rest. For SMD, use fine solder (0.5mm) and flux. For through-hole, insert the leads, bend them slightly, solder, and trim. Ensure no solder bridges between pins. Use a magnifier to check.

In Africa, components may be scarce. Salvage from dead boards: test with a multimeter before reuse. Store components in labeled bags or film canisters. For replacements, match voltage, capacitance, and tolerance. A 25V capacitor can replace a 16V one, but never lower. For resistors, 1/4W is common; for power, use 1W or higher.

After soldering, verify with a multimeter: check continuity, resistance, and voltage. If the board does not work, recheck orientation (diodes, electrolytic capacitors, ICs). A common mistake is reversed polarity. Take photos before removal to remember orientation.

lessons.title: Pad and Track Repair
lessons.body:
Pads and tracks can lift or break during rework. A lifted pad means the copper has separated from the board. To repair, first clean the area with alcohol. If the pad is still attached but lifted, you can glue it back with a tiny drop of superglue, then solder a thin wire from the pad to the track. If the pad is gone, you must create a new connection.

For a missing pad, find the track that connected to it. Scrape the green solder mask off the track near the break with a fiberglass pen or a sharp knife. Apply flux and tin the exposed copper. Then solder a thin insulated wire (30 AWG wire-wrap wire) from the track to the component lead. Use tweezers to route the wire neatly. Secure it with UV-curable solder mask or nail polish.

For broken tracks, use a jumper wire. If the track is on the surface, you can bridge the gap with a small piece of copper foil or a wire. For inner-layer breaks, it's often not repairable. In that case, run a wire on the surface. Always keep wires short and flat to avoid shorts.

Tools: fiberglass pen ($3), 30 AWG wire ($5), UV solder mask ($10). In Africa, you can use a toothbrush and acetone to clean. Avoid using too much heatâit causes more damage. Practice on scrap boards: deliberately lift a pad and repair it.

After repair, test continuity with a multimeter. Check that the repair is mechanically strongâtug gently on the wire. If the board is for a customer, document the repair with a photo. Pad repair is common in phone and laptop repair, where boards are dense. Patience and a steady hand are key.

lessons.title: Jumper Wires and Modifications
lessons.body:
Jumper wires are used to bypass broken tracks or add modifications. Use 30 AWG wire-wrap wire for signal lines and 24 AWG for power. Cut the wire to length, strip 1mm of insulation, and tin both ends. Solder one end to the source point and the other to the destination. Keep wires as short as possible and route them away from hot components.

For modifications, like adding an LED or changing a resistor value, plan first. Draw a simple schematic. Identify where to cut tracks (if needed) and where to solder. Use a sharp knife to cut a track, then verify with a multimeter that it's open. Add the new component and jumper wires. Secure wires with UV solder mask or hot glue.

In Africa, modifications are common in solar projects, car electronics, and phone repairs. For example, you might bypass a faulty charging IC by running a wire from the USB port to the battery. Always check polarity and voltage. Use a multimeter to confirm connections before powering up.

When soldering jumpers, use flux and a fine tip. Avoid excessive heat. If the wire is stranded, twist and tin it first. For high-current paths, use thicker wire and reinforce with solder. Label wires with a marker if multiple.

After modification, test thoroughly. Check for shorts between adjacent wires. If the device works, secure the wires with tape or glue. Document the modification with a photo and note. Remember, jumpers are a temporary fixâadvise the customer if it's not permanent. Practice on old boards by adding an LED with a resistor.

lessons.title: Rework Documentation and Verification
lessons.body:
Documenting your rework is essential for quality and traceability. After every repair, record: date, board model, fault, components replaced, and any jumpers or pad repairs. Use a notebook or a smartphone app. Take before and after photos. This helps if the device fails again and builds trust with customers.

Verification: After rework, visually inspect with a magnifier. Check for solder bridges, cold joints, and stray solder balls. Use a multimeter to test continuity, resistance, and voltage. Power up with a current-limited supply if possible. For simple devices, check that it functions as expected.

In Africa, where customer trust is crucial, show the customer the repair. Explain what you did. Provide a warrantyâeven 7 days. Keep a copy of the documentation. If you repair many devices, create a simple form: serial number, fault, action, parts used, technician name.

For complex repairs, test under load. For example, if you replaced a power transistor, run the device for 10 minutes and check temperature. If it gets too hot, recheck the solder joints. Use a thermal camera or your finger (carefully) to detect hot spots.

Finally, clean the board with isopropyl alcohol to remove flux. Flux residue can cause corrosion over time, especially in humid climates. Store repaired boards in anti-static bags. If you cannot test fully, note that in your documentation. Always follow up with the customer after a few days. Good documentation turns a one-time repair into a repeat customer.

quiz.q: What is the recommended temperature range for a temperature-controlled soldering iron used in rework?
quiz.explanation: Most soldering irons for electronics rework operate between 200Â°C and 450Â°C.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for removing solder from a through-hole joint?
quiz.explanation: A desoldering pump (solder sucker) is designed to vacuum molten solder from through-hole joints.

quiz.q: What should you do before desoldering a joint that looks oxidized?
quiz.explanation: Adding fresh solder improves heat transfer and helps the old solder melt evenly.

quiz.q: When using hot air to remove an SMD component, what airflow setting is generally recommended?
quiz.explanation: Low to medium airflow prevents blowing small components away.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of flux in desoldering?
options: B) To clean and improve heat transfer
quiz.explanation: Flux removes oxidation and helps solder flow better.

quiz.q: Which item is used to clean pads after desoldering?
quiz.explanation: Solder wick (desoldering braid) absorbs remaining solder from pads.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to remove a through-hole resistor?
options: B) Heat one leg at a time and gently lift
quiz.explanation: Heating one leg at a time and gently lifting prevents pad damage.

quiz.q: When replacing an electrolytic capacitor, what must you match?
quiz.explanation: Voltage and capacitance are critical for proper function and safety.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of a cold solder joint?
quiz.explanation: Cold joints look dull and lumpy and may not conduct reliably.

quiz.q: What tool can help you see small SMD components during rework?
options: B) Magnifying lamp or USB microscope
quiz.explanation: Magnification is essential for inspecting and placing small parts.

quiz.q: What should you do if a pad lifts during desoldering?
options: B) Stop and repair the pad
quiz.explanation: Continuing can cause more damage; repair the pad first.

quiz.q: Which wire gauge is typically used for jumper wires on signal lines?
quiz.explanation: 30 AWG wire-wrap wire is thin and ideal for signal jumpers.

quiz.q: What is the first step when repairing a missing pad?
options: B) Clean the area with alcohol
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes debris and oxidation, ensuring good adhesion.

quiz.q: How can you secure a jumper wire after soldering?
options: B) With UV solder mask or hot glue
quiz.explanation: UV solder mask or hot glue provides mechanical stability.

quiz.q: What should you do before cutting a track for a modification?
quiz.explanation: Planning with a schematic prevents mistakes.

quiz.q: Why is documentation important after rework?
options: B) For traceability and customer trust
quiz.explanation: Documentation helps track repairs and builds confidence.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean flux residue from a board?
quiz.explanation: Isopropyl alcohol safely removes flux without damaging the board.

quiz.q: What is a good practice after replacing a power transistor?
quiz.explanation: Testing under load ensures the repair works under real conditions.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safety precaution when using hot air?
options: A) Work in a ventilated area
quiz.explanation: Ventilation prevents inhaling harmful fumes.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of tinning a soldering iron tip?
quiz.explanation: Tinning protects the tip from oxidation and improves heat transfer.

quiz.q: When removing a QFN chip with hot air, how should you direct the nozzle?
quiz.explanation: Heating around the chip avoids blowing it off and ensures even melting.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of lifted pads?
quiz.explanation: Excessive heat or mechanical force can separate the pad from the board.

quiz.q: Which tool can help you inspect solder joints on a smartphone?
quiz.explanation: A USB microscope provides high magnification for small joints.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cannot test a repaired board fully?
quiz.explanation: Honest documentation notes any limitations of testing.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good conductor for repairing a broken track?
quiz.explanation: Copper wire is conductive and solderable.

quiz.q: What is the recommended way to store salvaged components?
quiz.explanation: Labeled bags prevent mix-ups and protect from moisture.

quiz.q: What does a multimeter measure?
quiz.explanation: A multimeter measures electrical properties like voltage and resistance.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using a file to clean a soldering iron tip?
quiz.explanation: Filing damages the protective plating, shortening tip life.

quiz.q: What is a jumper wire used for?
options: A) To bypass a broken track
quiz.explanation: Jumper wires restore electrical connections bypassing damaged tracks.

quiz.q: What should you do before powering up a modified board?
quiz.explanation: Checking for shorts prevents damage when power is applied.
